cloud.name: Cloud
cloud.def: Using computers, storage and services in a big data centre over the internet, and paying for what you use.

data-centre.name: Data centre
data-centre.def: A building full of computers, storage and networking that cloud providers run.

compute.name: Compute
compute.def: Computing power: machines or code that run your programs.

storage.name: Storage
storage.def: Space to keep files and data, such as reports, logs and pictures.

virtual-machine.name: Virtual machine
virtual-machine.def: A computer you rent in the cloud. It behaves like a real one but runs inside a bigger machine.

container.name: Container
container.def: A package that holds an app and what it needs, so it runs the same way anywhere.

access-control.name: Access control
access-control.def: Rules that decide who can see or change what.

devops.name: DevOps
devops.def: Ways of working that help the people who build software and the people who run it release changes often and safely.

ci-cd.name: CI/CD
ci-cd.def: Continuous integration and delivery: automatic testing of each change and automatic release when the tests pass.

version-control.name: Version control
version-control.def: A system that records every change to your files so you can look back or undo.

repository.name: Repository
repository.def: A project folder that also keeps the full history of changes.

commit.name: Commit
commit.def: A saved snapshot of your changes with a short message that says what changed.

deploy.name: Deploy
deploy.def: To put a new version of software where people can use it.

lessons.title: What is the Cloud?

cards.title: The cloud is someone else's computers
lines: The cloud means using computers in a big data centre over the internet.
You rent what you need. You do not buy and look after the machines.
Examples: Gmail, Google Drive and WhatsApp backups.

cards.title: Like power from the grid
lines: You do not build a power station for your house.
You plug in and pay for the units you use.
The cloud works the same way for computing.

cards.title: Three things you can rent
lines: Compute: machines that run programs.
Storage: space to keep files and data.
Services: ready-made tools such as databases and AI.

cards.title: Example: relay test reports
lines: A team saves test reports to cloud storage.
Engineers at different sites open the same files.
A script can check each new report.
Only store data you are allowed to store there.

cards.title: Why companies use it
lines: Start small and grow when needed.
Pay for use, not for idle machines.
The provider handles backups and keeps the hardware running.

cards.title: Limits to know
lines: It needs an internet connection.
Costs can grow if you forget to switch things off.
You must control who can see your data.
Some sites cannot use public cloud because of rules.

cards.title: Control systems are different
lines: Protection and control systems must stay reliable and secure.
Never connect live substation equipment to the internet without an approved design.
Analysing a copy of data in the cloud is different from controlling equipment.
Follow your company's cyber-security and data rules.

cards.title: Practice: cloud or not?
lines: List 3 apps you use every day that run in the cloud.
For each, say what is stored or run there.
Example: WhatsApp backup stores your chat history.

cards.title: Recap
lines: The cloud is rented computing over the internet.
You rent compute, storage and services.
Control who sees data, and watch the cost.

quiz.q: What is the cloud?
options: Rented computers and services reached over the internet
quiz.why: The cloud means using a provider's computers and services over the internet.

quiz.q: Which is the best electrical comparison?
options: Taking power from the grid and paying for use
quiz.why: Cloud computing is rented and metered, like grid power.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the three things you can rent?
quiz.why: Cloud offers compute, storage and services.

quiz.q: A risk of cloud use is...
options: Costs can grow if resources are left running
quiz.why: Unused resources still cost money, so switch them off and set budget alerts.

quiz.q: Is it safe to connect live substation equipment to the internet?
options: Only with an approved design and your company's rules
Yes, if the AI says so
quiz.why: Protection and control systems need approved, secure designs.

lessons.career: Most modern engineering tools, including AI tools, run in the cloud. Knowing the basics helps you talk with IT teams and use these tools safely.

lessons.title: Cloud Building Blocks

cards.title: Four blocks make a cloud service
lines: Compute, storage, database and network.
Security, monitoring and billing sit around all four.
Almost every cloud service is made from these.

cards.title: Compute
lines: A virtual machine is a computer you rent.
A function runs a small piece of code only when needed.
A container packs an app so it runs the same everywhere.

cards.title: Storage
lines: Object storage keeps files such as PDFs and CSVs.
It is cheap and easy to share.
Good for reports and logs.

cards.title: Databases
lines: A database keeps data in organised tables.
You can search and filter it quickly.
Example: a table of relay test results.

cards.title: Network and access
lines: Rules decide who can reach what.
Keep private data private.
Use strong passwords and two-step login.

cards.title: Mapping to your world
lines: The table links each block to something you know.

head: Block
Plain meaning
Relay-world example
rows: A script that checks test reports
Folder of PDF reports and CSV results
Table of operating times by relay
Only the test team can open reports

cards.title: The big three providers
lines: Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud are the main ones.
They offer the same ideas with different names.
Learn the ideas first. Choose one provider later.

cards.title: Keys, costs and cleanup
lines: Never put passwords or keys in public code.
Set a budget alert before you try anything.
Delete what you do not use.

cards.title: Practice: draw the blocks
lines: Draw four boxes and name them.
Write one relay-related example inside each.

cards.title: Recap
lines: Compute, storage, database, network.
Security and cost sit around them.
Learn the ideas, then choose a provider.

quiz.q: Which block keeps files such as PDFs and CSVs?
quiz.why: Object storage holds files.

quiz.q: What is a virtual machine?
options: A rented computer in the cloud
quiz.why: It behaves like a real computer but runs inside a larger machine.

quiz.q: What does a container do?
options: Packs an app so it runs the same everywhere
quiz.why: Containers bundle an app with what it needs.

quiz.q: Where should passwords and keys NOT be placed?
quiz.why: Never put secrets in public code.

quiz.q: What should you set up before experimenting?
quiz.why: Budget alerts stop surprise bills.

lessons.title: What is DevOps?

cards.title: DevOps in one sentence
lines: DevOps helps people who build software and people who run it work as one team.
The goal: release small changes often and safely.

cards.title: Commissioning, but for software
lines: You test a relay before you energise it.
You check, record, then switch on.
DevOps tests and checks software before it goes live, again and again.

cards.title: The loop
lines: Plan, code, test, release, monitor, learn.
Then plan the next small change.
Small steps are safer than one huge change.

cards.title: Four key habits
lines: Version control: record every change.
Automated tests: check each change by machine.
CI/CD: test and release automatically.
Monitoring: watch the live system.

cards.title: Example: a report checker
lines: You write a script that checks relay test reports.
Each change is saved in Git.
Tests confirm it still works.
Then it is published automatically.

cards.title: Why it matters for AI apps
lines: AI apps change often: prompts, data and models.
DevOps keeps each change tracked and reversible.
You can see what changed when something goes wrong.

cards.title: For engineering work
lines: Software that touches protection or control needs strict approval.
Never push untested changes to live systems.
Follow your company's change-control process.

cards.title: Practice: match the loop
lines: Write the six steps of the loop.
Next to each, write what you did when you built this website.
Example: release = uploaded files to GitHub.

cards.title: Recap
lines: DevOps is teamwork for safe, small, frequent releases.
Record, test, release, monitor.
Live protection and control systems need approved change control.

quiz.q: What is the main goal of DevOps?
options: Release small changes often and safely
quiz.why: Small, safe, frequent releases are the goal.

quiz.q: Which is the best comparison?
quiz.why: Both check carefully before switching on.

quiz.q: What does version control do?
options: Records every change so you can undo
quiz.why: It keeps a history of changes.

quiz.q: What does CI/CD do?
quiz.why: CI/CD automates testing and release.

quiz.q: Can you push untested changes to a live protection system?
quiz.why: Live protection and control systems need strict approval.

lessons.title: Your Own DevOps: GitHub and GitHub Pages

cards.title: You already did DevOps
lines: You created a repository.
You committed files.
GitHub Pages published your site.
That is version control plus automatic release.

cards.title: Repository and commit
lines: A repository is a project folder with its full history.
A commit is a saved snapshot with a short message.
Each commit says what changed and when.

cards.title: A logbook for your project
lines: A commissioning log records each step and who did it.
Git does the same for your files.
You can look back and undo.

cards.title: Deploy
lines: To deploy is to put a new version online.
On GitHub Pages, a commit to the main branch publishes your site.
Wait one or two minutes, then refresh.

cards.title: A safe update habit
lines: Change one thing at a time.
Write a clear commit message.
Check the live site on your phone.
If it breaks, go back to the last good version.

cards.title: Example: test scripts and settings backups
lines: Teams keep test scripts in version control.
Each change shows who changed it, when and why.
Never keep confidential settings or customer data in a public repository.

cards.title: Do not publish secrets
lines: Do not upload passwords, API keys or company files to a public repository.
Public means anyone in the world can read it.
If you upload a secret by mistake, change it immediately.

cards.title: Practice: read your history
lines: Open your repository on GitHub.
Find the list of commits.
Read the last three messages.
Write what each one changed.

cards.title: Recap
lines: Repository, commit, deploy: you already use all three.
Small changes, clear messages, check the live site.
Never publish secrets.

quiz.q: What is a commit?
options: A saved snapshot of changes with a message
quiz.why: A commit records what changed.

quiz.q: What does deploying mean?
quiz.why: Deploying makes the new version available to users.

quiz.q: Which is safe to put in a public repository?
quiz.why: Public repositories can be read by anyone. Keep secrets out.

quiz.q: What should you do when an update breaks your site?
options: Go back to the last good version
quiz.why: Version control lets you go back.

quiz.q: Why write clear commit messages?
options: They explain what changed and why
quiz.why: Good messages make the history useful.
